scenes.text: Someone texts you, are you coming tonight? [1] And your phone suggests, yes, I'll be there, before you type a single letter. [2] Let's break down how smart replies work.

Here's what happens, in the blink of an eye. [1] A message arrives, are you coming tonight? [2] A small language model reads it, along with the recent chat. [3] It predicts a few likely short replies. [4] A filter removes anything odd or unsafe, [5] and you see three quick options.

data.heading: In the blink of an eye

scenes.text: Many phones do this with an on-device model. [1] That means the AI runs directly on your phone, not on a server in the cloud. [2] So it's faster, [3] it can work without internet, [4] and your messages can stay on your device.

data.definition: AI that runs directly on your phone instead of a server in the cloud.

scenes.text: Remember next word prediction, from episode two? [1] The model scores possible replies. Yes is the most likely, running late is less likely, and can't today, even less. [2] It picks the top few, [3] and when you tap one, it can even suggest how to finish your sentence.

So what makes a good suggestion? [1] It's short, because it's just one tap. [2] It's relevant to the message, and your chat. [3] It matches your style, casual or formal. [4] And it's safe, never rude or embarrassing.
So where will you see it? [1] Gmail's smart reply, and smart compose. [2] Keyboard suggestions on Android and iPhone. [3] And quick replies in messaging apps.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think smart replies mean someone, or some giant AI, is reading every message. [2] Often, it's a small model running on your own phone, predicting a few likely words. No human is reading along.

data.myth: Someone is reading my messages to suggest replies.
data.fact: Often it's a small model on your own phone, predicting a few likely words.
